fields.body: مسجد الحبیش، ہفوف کے وسط میں، محلہ جنوبی الرفعہ میں واقع ہے۔ یہ الاحساء کی قدیم ترین تاریخی مساجد میں سے ایک ہے، اور تیرہویں صدی ہجری (تقریباً انیسویں صدی عیسوی) میں تعمیر ہوئی۔ اسے مسجد شیخ عبد العزیز العلجی بھی کہتے ہیں۔ وہ فقہ اور نحو میں الاحساء کے بڑے علما میں سے تھے، اور ان کے درس اسی مسجد میں ہوتے تھے۔ یہ مسجد چونے کے پتھر اور مٹی سے بنی ہے، اور اس کی چھت شندل نامی لکڑی (جو کبھی خلیجی خطے میں درآمد کی جاتی تھی)، بانس اور چٹائیوں کی ہے۔ گول محرابوں والا برآمدہ اور شمال مشرقی کونے پر چوکور مینار اس کی پہچان ہیں۔ اس کا کل رقبہ تقریباً 318 مربع میٹر ہے، اور اس میں تقریباً نوے نمازیوں کی گنجائش ہے۔ 2020 میں “شہزادہ محمد بن سلمان منصوبے” کے پہلے مرحلے میں اس کی بحالی ہوئی۔ یہ تاریخی مساجد کے لیے ایک ترقیاتی منصوبہ ہے۔ یوں یہ مسجد پھر سے آباد ہو گئی، اور اس کے اصل خدوخال برقرار رہے۔

blind_reader_rulings.reason: The rows are the source's, in both languages, on hubaish, umzurainiq and abubakr-mosque: 'Entry: a working mosque, no entry fee', the owner's fixed row, 'Fees: free entry' — the three rows of jabri-mosque, value for value, and approved pairs of the translation memory reused verbatim. Two of them say that nothing is charged, and the row labelled Entry answers with a working mosque. The reader's remedy (the Entry row to say only that the mosque is in use) is a change of the source's row and is on record for the owner. Logged; nothing is merged or dropped in the Urdu. b3's reader said the same of dibs.

Serious, and the source's and the template's, not the Urdu's. hubaish, umzurainiq and abubakr-mosque carry no Hours row and none of the five pages has an operator link, so the template's notice (the interface string det.hoursNotice, ruled under P27 and final in b0-ui) speaks of hours a card does not show and of a management nobody names. Whether a working mosque may be entered between prayers is the owner's unanswered question: the Urdu states no time, neither affirming nor denying, and the fixed row is his string. Nothing is said of women visitors in either language. The reader himself calls it missing information and asks for no wording. Logged second among the defects; nothing is supplied.

Not a leaf of this batch: the notice is the interface string det.hoursNotice, final in b0-ui and a pair of the translation memory; its word for those who run a place is one word for every kind of attraction. Recorded for the next interface round: on a small neighbourhood mosque the word sounds like an office to this reader, and the mention of fees straight under 'free entry' made him wonder for a second whether a fee is sometimes charged. That the template prints the notice under a card with no hours and no named operator is logged with observation 2.

The owner's fixed point, not this judge's to change: the label is ruling N17 (one source label, one Urdu rendering on every mosque page) and the row under it is the owner's string, final by his decision of 2026-10-13; the card heading is the interface string det.visitInfo, final in b0-ui. Recorded for him, not ruled away: this is the fifth reader in two rounds to hear something devotional in the label on an ordinary mosque ('made me briefly think the place is treated as a shrine'), and he counts three words for the same people on one page. The third of them, the body's phrase for visitors to the district, is item N60 and is not the mosque's visitors.

No fault in the wording ('reads naturally and politely'), and the row is the owner's string, with the dress phrase he chose on 2026-10-13 knowing that it says a little less than the source's 'modest'. What is expected of women and children is said by neither source and is not supplied. Recorded for the owner with observation 4.

Not a leaf of this batch: the button is the interface string share.btn, ruled in b0-ui (item N3: the native wording against the commoner loan) and final there. Recorded for the next interface round: understood, bookish to this reader, whose phone says the loan.

The four builds are the sources' own four wordings of the area line, each carried by its rule: where the source names a larger place as a bare name it leads (ruling P20: tahimiyah-e, abubakr-mosque), and where it gives a place and then its position the source's order is kept (item N30, ruled by b3's judge in this round: hubaish, umzurainiq); uqair-mosque's line is the approved line of uqair-castle from the translation memory. No line is faulted in itself; the unevenness between pages is logged for the owner, as item N30 says, to even out in the source.

The split is the English source's own, field by field: twelve kilometres, forty, around eleven, about fifty, some ninety and thirty are words there; 318, 214, 94 and 125 are figures (the same holds in the Arabic). The round's practice, checked at every stage, is that a number the English writes as a word is a word in the Urdu and a figure stays a figure, so that every figure can be matched against its source. The 'about' before an exact figure is the source's as well ('about 318 square metres', 'some 94 worshippers', 'only around eleven'). Not changed in one batch; logged as a matter of the sources' style, as b3's judge logged it.

The sources say it so: 2017 and 2020 are given in the Gregorian calendar alone, the first phase of the same Project is 'in 2020' on hubaish and '1441 AH / 2020 CE' on abubakr-mosque, and umzurainiq's second phase has no year in either language. Nothing is converted, computed or carried from one page to another (ruling N12); the century pair of hubaish is in the form item N36 rules. Logged.

The two sentences are approved text, reused verbatim: ruling N16, point 3 a (final after three rounds and five readers on jawatha-mosque) — the short name as the press writes it, inflected, inside quotation marks, and what the programme is for in a clause of its own with the source's preposition. A ruling is not reopened and a pair of the translation memory is not broken on one reader. Recorded for whoever may reopen it, and charged under nativeness on the three pages: this reader could not tell where the proper name ends, because the inflected noun stands inside the marks; the explanation lands as a flat sentence; and its adjective is to him the word for roads and drains. That the same two sentences stand on three pages is the source's (the Project's full name on each).

Three names and two verbs, each the source's: umzurainiq's summary says 'restored under the historic mosques project' and its body 'rehabilitated within the second phase of the Prince Mohammed bin Salman Project', in both languages; uqair-mosque says 'restored under the historic mosques restoration programme'. No page says whether these are one scheme, and the Urdu does not say so; the two Urdu verbs are kept apart as the two source verbs are (restored / rehabilitated), never crossed. Logged.

The title is the pattern item N43 rules for both tahimiyah pages (b3's judge, binding here) and translates what title_en translates; the second name on abubakr-mosque is the source's own, translated by the English ('also known as the Eastern Mosque'), and takes no quotation marks (ruling N16, point 5). Two mosques in two places carry the same describing name in both sources; nothing in the Urdu can tell them apart without adding to one of them. Recorded as the stated cost of N43, and charged under fit on tahimiyah-e: the title reads to him as a description, not as what people call the mosque.

Ruling P17, not reopened: the name is written as the Arabic writes it, with no vowel sign and no pronunciation gloss (the build guard of P8 rejects the signs). b3's reader said the same of the same name. Charged under fit.

The source says exactly this and no more: 'also known as the First Tahimiyah Mosque'. The Urdu says that people also call it so, which marks it as a name and makes no claim that it was the first built; a second name takes no quotation marks (ruling N16, point 5). Whether the name records a fact is said by neither language. Minor; recorded in the entry.

Applied for what is the Urdu's own (change 0): the name and the funeral prayers are one sentence again, as in the English. NOT supplied: the link he guessed — the Arabic alone gives the prayers as the reason for the name, and neither language says what the name means; Arabic-only content is not imported. NOT supplied either: whether prayers are held here today. Neither source says so, this card has no 'working mosque' row where three others have one, and it touches the owner's unanswered question. Both are logged among the source defects.

The collocation is Urdu's own for exactly this statement (the exact phrase stands on 7 reference pages, of a region and of a craft among them) and is word for word what both sources say: 'its history goes back centuries'. His wording says that the building is centuries old, which is a little more than the sources say of a mud structure. That no century is given is the source's. His remark that it sounds slightly foreign to him is counted under nativeness.

Applied (change 1): the circular relative clause is gone. The sentence is the one b3's judge ruled for jalaniyah and tahimiyah-e together (item N46-listed-among-registered-historic-mosques), copied by script. Who keeps the list is said by neither source and is not supplied.

Applied for the lost antecedent (change 2): the mountain is named, as the source names it in that very sentence. Not changed: that the page says twice that the mountain is near, and that it ends on 'an easy stop', are the source's sentence in both languages (logged); nothing is added to say why one would stop.

The two rows are the source's: the owner's fixed row, and an Hours row that holds no hours ('Open to visitors during daylight hours'), on both tahimiyah pages; and this card has no Entry row because its source has none. The wording of the Hours value is item N41 (b3's ruling, one string on both pages). That an Hours row stands on a mosque page against the owner's own rule is logged for him; nothing is supplied.
No fault reported: the description of the building reads well and he can picture it. Nothing to apply.

The name is half translated in the source itself ('South Al-Rifaa'), and the Urdu does what the English does, which is also what the one Urdu reference page on this mosque does (item N63). Whether the direction is part of the name cannot be shown without the Arabic adjective, which an Urdu reader takes for an opaque word. Minor; recorded in the entry.

Applied for the verb (change 3). NOT applied, the larger half: 'one of the oldest' stands in both sources on hubaish (thirteenth century AH), on abubakr-mosque (some three centuries) and on the approved jabri-mosque (ninth century AH); a superlative is a claim and follows the Arabic (ruling P19). That the three together empty the word is the sources' and is logged.

The clause is the owner's, not this judge's: his ruling of 2026-10-02 (build checks C40 and C41) puts the explanation in a bracket directly after the word, and the Urdu is the clause approved on qasr-ibrahim, reused byte for byte. The wood's name is the termbase's, built from the Arabic spelling. Recorded for the owner, and charged under fit on hubaish: the bracket breaks into a list of three and he lost the thread before the verb; and the name looks to him like a misspelling of the Urdu word for sandalwood, so that he could not tell which wood the roof is made of.

Ruling N34, not reopened by a batch judge: the arch is the one word, marked on a mosque page by the plural, and no other word is brought in for it. The mark is in place on both pages and did not do its work for this reader: on hubaish he pictured several prayer niches in a veranda before he worked out that arches are meant, and on umzurainiq he still cannot tell. He is the third reader of this round to take the plural for niches (both readers of b3 did on jalaniyah). Recorded under item N42 for whoever may reopen N34, and charged under nativeness on both pages. No niche is named on either page, so item N42 moves nothing.

The source's: 'it regained its life as a working mosque' (Arabic: life returned to it) on a page that has not said the mosque had fallen out of use. The Urdu says as much as the English and no more; nothing is added to explain it. Logged.

Item N59, ruled on this observation: the word is the Arabic's own and the Urdu name of the subject beside fiqh and exegesis (the exact pairing stands on 12 reference pages, and the Urdu reference article on this very sheikh uses it). The reader knew it; his doubt is for other readers. The general word for grammar would read beside fiqh as 'rules', and every fuller form adds a word the source lacks. Minor; recorded.
No fault reported: apart from the items above the page reads clearly. Nothing to apply.
Ruling P17, not reopened: no vowel sign and no pronunciation gloss is added to a name; no source says how the second word is said or what it means. Charged under fit on umzurainiq.

Both sources say exactly this, in summary and body, and neither gives the cemetery's name (the Arabic slug alone suggests it). The Urdu repeats the statement where the source repeats it and completes nothing. Logged.

Serious, and the source's, in both languages: 'a small historic mosque', 'restored' in the summary, and a rehabilitation 'expanding it from a mere thirty square metres to around 214, with room for some 94 worshippers'. The Urdu carries each statement at its strength with the source's figures. One thing the Urdu did, on record since stage 4: the English gives no unit after 214 and the Arabic says metres without 'square'; the Urdu writes square metres, a repair of form under ruling P23. Logged third among the defects, with the harm: the visitor cannot tell whether he will see a century-old mosque or a new building. Nothing is reconciled.

Applied, second half (change 4): the verb is the one the neighbouring pages use. NOT applied, first half: the word for gypsum plaster is a verified termbase entry (the dictionary's word for wall plaster; the loans are barred by the owner's rule P16) and is one key in both batches; a sourced entry is not overruled on a minor remark. Recorded in the entry: he had to guess it, and b3's second reader stopped on it as well.

The repeated word is the source's 'distinguished by … and by …', which stage 1 split so that the hallmark has a sentence of its own; the chain of three possessives is 'a hallmark of the Eastern Province's mosque architecture' and every shorter wording changes what is claimed (stage 4 weighed it). The country of the province is not named by the page in either language and is not supplied. Minor; counted under nativeness.
No fault reported: the two sentences read as real Urdu and he liked them. Nothing to apply; recorded as a pass for the ruled word for a mosque in use (ruling N26).

Serious, and the source's and the owner's: by his ruling of 2026-10-02 (build check C29, clause d) this card carries no visiting row; its first row is 'Site status' and speaks of the port complex, and the second says 'Free entry' of something it does not name. Whether the mosque itself is open, whether one may go in or pray there, whether there are hours, and how far the port is, are said by neither language. The Urdu of the row is item N55 and promises nothing. Logged first among the defects, with the harm in the reader's own words: he would not drive a family to the coast on this card. Nothing is supplied.

The source's, in both languages, and the owner's ruling: the body says the mosque was restored; the card says works are under way in the port complex. The Urdu keeps the two subjects apart as the source does (the mosque in the body, the complex in the card) and adds no bridge. Logged with observation 34.

Applied in both fields (changes 5 and 8): the verb is now said of the parts of the port, of which Urdu says it, and the echo of one root in the body is gone. NOT supplied: whether the mosque was built in that reign or stood before it and was improved — the summary says 'developed' and the body 'built and developed', in both languages (logged) — and a date for the mosque, which no source gives.

Applied (change 6): the subject comes first and the pronoun that sent him back is gone, in the frame of the approved opening of uqair-castle. Not changed: 'historic' twice is the source's (the historic port, the port's historic mosque); the two now stand a clause apart.
Applied in the structure of his own sentence (change 7), with the approved wording of the sister page for the gateway. NOT supplied: what Najd is — the source names it and no more.

The sentence is the owner's claim in the one Urdu wording approved for it on al-uqair and uqair-castle (build check C34: 'the first seaport in the east of the Kingdom', never 'the oldest port'); how the site states one of its own claims is not changed on a reader's remark (the role file's rule, with rulings P24 and P25), and the pair is reused byte for byte. 'Seaport' is the source's word in both languages. Recorded for the owner: the compound sounds redundant to this reader, and the present tense beside 'historic port' left him unsure whether ships still call.

Ruling N35, final and not reopened: the source names whose building it is and nothing else, and the one Urdu word that would tell the reader more says a seat or a palace, which the site rule on Al-Uqair bars. The cost that ruling states is met again — the two look-alike words side by side were misread on first pass — and is charged under nativeness and fit on this page, as it was on uqair-castle. For the owner, as N35 says: the remedy is in the source, a word saying what the building was.

The sentence is the source's own, element for element: 'restored' and 'restoration', 'historic mosques' twice, the Royal Commission as the supporter, and no year. The Urdu drops none of them and adds none; the Commission's name is the form item N44 rules (b3's judge), and the two verbs for repair are never crossed. Missing in both languages and not supplied: when the restoration happened, and why a commission of two other cities appears. Recorded under N44: this reader could not tell at once that the name holds two place names (b3's first reader read it without a remark). The weight of the sentence is counted under nativeness. Logged.
Applied (change 9): the two words that ran together are parted by 'its', which the source has. His own wording is not taken whole, because it changes the source's noun for the visitors.

The source's, in both languages: the body tells the port's story and says of the mosque only where it stands, who prayed in it, that it is among the port's facilities and that it was restored — no size, material, look, age or year. Nothing is carried over from another page. Logged; the reader calls it missing.
No fault reported: the sentence reads well, a little literary and natural. Nothing to apply.

Applied in summary and body (changes 11 and 12), in the structure of his own remedy. NOT changed: the family name with its article is the Arabic's spelling and a termbase key (ruling N27: a family name keeps its article); that it first reads to him as the common word for a cleric with an article is charged under fit.

Applied in the summary (change 10; item N58). NOT applied in the body: 'one of the oldest mosques of Al-Ahsa's heritage' is the possessive frame approved on qasr-ibrahim and read there by three readers; it does not use the construction he heard as inheritance. Whether 'heritage' means an official register or simply age is said by neither source. His remark on the body is recorded under N58 and counted under nativeness.

The sources differ on a fact and the Arabic is the authority (item N57): the house and the schools are Sheikh Abi Bakr's in the Arabic and 'the Al-Mulla family's' in the English, and neither language says who he is or how he stands to the Sheikh Muhammad bin Abi Bakr of the title. The two spellings are one name in two cases, as Urdu writes them: the genitive inside the full name after the word for 'son of', the citation form where the kunya stands alone. Whether the house and schools still stand is said by neither source. Logged fifth among the defects; nothing is explained.

The source says 'in the heart of' in summary and body, where the other pages' sources say 'central'; the Urdu keeps the two apart as the sources do. The phrase is the one approved on sahood and read there by three readers. Minor; recorded.

Both sources say exactly this, in this order: the Project's first phase with its year, then the traditional character kept 'while accommodating around 125 worshippers'. The capacity comes last because the source puts it last; the year belongs to the phase, as the Arabic makes plain. Minor; nothing is reordered on taste.
No fault reported beyond the phrase of observation 45, which is answered there: the sentence reads well and gives the place its character. Nothing to apply.

Interface strings of b0-ui (det.nearby.h, det.nearby.d, det.nearby.note), final there and pairs of the translation memory. Recorded for the next interface round: the heading is a little brochure-like to a third reader (after b2's and b3's), and the tail of the distance note reads to this one as an afterthought.

source_defects.where: uqair-mosque: the card, and the card against the body (observations 34 serious, 35)
source_defects.defect: By the owner's ruling of 2026-10-02 this mosque's card has no visiting row. Its first row, 'Site status', speaks of the port complex ('undergoing restoration work, and some parts may be closed'); its second says 'Free entry' without saying of what. Neither language says whether the mosque itself is open or among the closed parts, whether one may go in or pray there, whether the compound has hours, or how far the port lies from Hofuf. The body says the mosque 'was restored' while the card says works are under way.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Both rows are carried as they stand (item N55) and no visiting row is supplied; the body says nothing of works under way. HARM, the greatest in the batch: this is the farthest of the five places, and the reader 'would not drive a family to the coast on this card'. FOR THE OWNER: one line saying whether the mosque can be entered while the works last.

source_defects.where: hubaish, umzurainiq, abubakr-mosque, tahimiyah-e: the card and the template's notice (observations 2 serious, 3)
source_defects.defect: Three of the four have no Hours row; none of the five pages has an operator link; the template still prints its notice that hours and fees may change and that one should confirm with the management of the place. No page says whether a visitor who is not coming to pray may enter between prayers, and none says anything of women visitors or of a women's section.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The owner's fixed row and the notice stand as approved; no time is stated, affirmed or denied. HARM: a family cannot plan an hour for any of the three town mosques and has nobody to ask. FOR THE OWNER: his pending question on working mosques, and an operator contact or no notice where a card has no hours.

source_defects.defect: The page calls the mosque 'small' and 'historic', says in the summary that it was 'restored', and then that its rehabilitation expanded it 'from a mere thirty square metres to around 214, with room for some 94 worshippers' — seven times the size, and more worshippers than the 318 square metres of hubaish hold. The English gives no unit after 214; the Arabic says metres without 'square'. Both languages say twice that the mosque is named after the cemetery beside it and never give the cemetery's name.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each statement is carried at its strength with the source's figures. MENDED IN FORM under ruling P23: the unit after 214 is written, «214 مربع میٹر»; the literal wording, if the owner prefers it until the source is repaired, is the figure alone. HARM: the reader no longer knows whether he would see a century-old mosque or a mostly new building, and distrusts the word 'historic'.

source_defects.defect: An Hours row on a mosque page, against the owner's rule that no visiting time is stated for a working mosque; it holds no hours ('Open to visitors during daylight hours'), repeats the row above it and does not say whether one may go inside. Everything the body says of prayer is in the past, the card has no 'working mosque' row where three other cards have one, and neither language says whether prayers are held today. The same two rows stand on tahimiyah-s (b3).
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Rendered as the source has it, the value by item N41; nothing is tied to prayer times. HARM: the reader does not know whether this is a mosque in use or an empty old building. FOR THE OWNER: with his pending question.

source_defects.where: abubakr-mosque: body, the house and the schools (observation 47); title against slug
source_defects.defect: 'Near the house and religious schools of the Al-Mulla family' in the English; near the house of Sheikh Abi Bakr and his religious schools in the Arabic. Neither language says who Sheikh Abi Bakr is, how he stands to the Sheikh Muhammad bin Abi Bakr of the title, or whether the house and schools can still be seen. The English writes 'the Al-Mulla family' where the Arabic has the longer family name; the Arabic slug calls the mosque by the father's name.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The Arabic's fact is followed (item N57): «شیخ ابو بکر کے گھر اور ان کے دینی مدارس کے قریب». The reader met a person brought in as if he knew him. FOR THE OWNER: one of the two languages to be brought into line, and a word saying who the sheikh is.

source_defects.defect: The body tells the port's story and almost nothing of the mosque: no size, material, look, age, or year of restoration. The summary says the facilities were 'developed under King Abdulaziz' (in the Arabic the King developed them), the body that they were 'built and developed' in his reign, so that the reader cannot tell whether the mosque was built then. The restoration sentence says 'restored … restoration … historic mosques … historic mosques' in one breath and names the Royal Commission for Jubail and Yanbu as a supporter without a word on why; the mosque is placed twice (first and last sentence).
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Carried as it is; nothing is brought from another page. In summary and body 'facilities' is said as the parts of the port, of which Urdu says 'developed' (changes 5 and 8); the literal noun, on record for the owner: «تعمیرات». HARM: on four pages the reader could picture the building; here he cannot.

source_defects.where: umzurainiq summary against its body; uqair-mosque; hubaish, abubakr-mosque; jalaniyah (observation 11)
source_defects.defect: The mosque-restoration schemes have another name on almost every page: 'the historic mosques project' and, in the same page's body, 'the Prince Mohammed bin Salman Project for the Development of Historic Mosques' (umzurainiq); 'the historic mosques restoration programme' (uqair-mosque); 'the historic mosques care programme' (jabri-mosque). 'Restored' in one field and 'rehabilitated' in the next. The Royal Commission supports a programme here and restores a mosque itself on jalaniyah. No page says how any of these relate.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each name and each verb as its own field has it: three Urdu descriptions and one named Project, two verbs never crossed. The reader could not tell whether they are one scheme.

source_defects.where: hubaish, abubakr-mosque (and the approved jabri-mosque): 'one of the oldest'; hubaish body (observations 22, 25)
source_defects.defect: 'One of Al-Ahsa's oldest historic mosques' of a mosque of the thirteenth century AH, 'one of Al-Ahsa's oldest heritage mosques' of one some three centuries old, and the same of jabri-mosque, older by four centuries. hubaish 'regained its life as a working mosque' without having said that it had fallen out of use; no date is given for the sheikh whose lessons it hosted.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each superlative under its 'one of', as the Arabic has it (ruling P19); 'again in use' as the source says it. Read together the claim stops meaning anything to the reader, and 'again' is left hanging.

source_defects.where: hubaish, umzurainiq, abubakr-mosque: the card; the Fees row of all five (observation 1)
source_defects.defect: 'Entry: a working mosque, no entry fee' and 'Fees: free entry' say one thing twice, in both languages, and the row labelled Entry answers with a working mosque. A Fees row stands on every mosque page. The cards of the five pages do not match one another (an Hours row on one, an Entry row on three, a status row on one).
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The approved pairs of the translation memory, verbatim. The reader stopped to check whether the two rows were about two different things.

source_defects.where: the five bodies: years and numbers (observations 9, 8)
source_defects.defect: The first phase of one Project is 'in 2020' on hubaish and '1441 AH / 2020 CE' on abubakr-mosque; the second phase on umzurainiq has no year; 2017 and 2020 stand in the Gregorian calendar alone beside a Hijri century. Some measures are words (twelve kilometres, about fifty, some ninety, thirty square metres) and others figures (318, 214, 94, 125), within one sentence on umzurainiq; 'about' stands before exact figures.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Nothing is converted, computed or evened out (ruling N12); the Urdu follows the English field by field, so the unevenness shows across pages and inside one sentence.

source_defects.defect: The earlier name: the English describes ('where funeral prayers were held'), the Arabic gives the prayers as the reason for the name, and neither says what the name means. 'The First Tahimiyah Mosque': a name, with no word on whether it was the first built. The page says twice that the mountain is near. Its title's 'East Mosque' and the 'Eastern Mosque' given as a second name on abubakr-mosque are one phrase for two mosques.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The name and the prayers are one sentence, as in the English, and no reason is stated; the mountain is named both times, as in the source; the two names stand as the sources have them. The reader guessed the reason for the earlier name, and wondered for a moment whether two pages were about one mosque.

source_defects.where: the area rows of the five pages (observation 7)
source_defects.defect: The sources word the area line four ways: village, then the larger places (tahimiyah-e); district, then its position in the town (hubaish, umzurainiq); district, then the town (abubakr-mosque); a port, then a description of the coast (uqair-mosque).
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: Each line by its rule: a larger place named bare leads (ruling P20); a place followed by its position keeps the source's order (item N30). The reader had to re-orient at each row. FOR THE OWNER: to even out in the source, as item N30 says.

source_defects.where: hubaish: summary; body, the chandal bracket in the Arabic
source_defects.defect: Both summaries name 'South Al-Rifaa' with nothing to say that it is a district, and no town. The Arabic chandal bracket lacks the noun the qasr-ibrahim bracket has.
source_defects.effect_on_urdu: The summary stands bare, as its own field has it (item N61); the option for the owner is the district word before the name, «محلہ جنوبی الرفعہ میں». The chandal clause is the approved one, byte for byte.

source_defects.where: remarks on the owner's fixed points and on ruled claims, recorded for him (observations 4, 5, 23, 39, 40)
source_defects.defect: Not defects of the source. (1) The visiting row: the label first suggests a devotional visit to a shrine (fifth reader in two rounds), and with the value's word for visitors and the card heading's he counts three words for one idea; 'suitable dress' is not defined for women and children.
